stumbles.quote: I am certain you can find a way to make use of this and build upon our prior work.
stumbles.why: "Our prior work" refers to an earlier project/version the text never describes. Who "Oskar" is and what the prior work was are unexplained.

stumbles.quote: I assumed its main use for remex would be faster training
stumbles.why: "remex" is never explained. We can't tell whether it is a library, a quantizer or an index. Later it has "1-bit quantization" and "hash cells", but the text never says what it is.

stumbles.quote: e-means reaches the error of 25 iterations of Lloyd's k-means in 1 to 3 passes.
stumbles.why: e-means is never described. The text doesn't say what a "pass" is or how it compares with a Lloyd iteration. The paper is cited only by its arXiv number.

stumbles.quote: On 4 CPUs that is 1.6 to 10.2 times sooner.
stumbles.why: It is unclear whether this speedup is wall-clock time and what k is. The 1.6–10.2 range doesn't say which cases produce which end.

stumbles.quote: the centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector
stumbles.why: A 4,096-centroid table is fixed in size. Dividing it across 100,000 vectors gives 126 bytes only for a particular dimension and dtype, which the text never states. The comparison to "a second bit per dimension" can't be checked without the dimension.

stumbles.quote: Adding a second bit per dimension would cost less than that.
stumbles.why: It is unclear whether this is a claim about cost only, or whether it also reaches similar recall. The conclusion that offset coding is not worth it isn't actually stated.

stumbles.quote: A search that scans 0.56% of the corpus finds 90% of the true neighbours.
stumbles.why: The text doesn't say how many cells are probed. 0.56% is about 23 of 4,096 cells, which is far less than one cell's share if probing is uniform. It doesn't say whether this is recall@10 or whether it involves reranking. The number of cells probed is a gap, and 0.56% looks suspiciously small for balanced cells.

stumbles.quote: remex's hash cells find 70% while scanning 34%.
stumbles.why: It is unclear whether this is the same recall measure as the 90% figure, so the comparison can't be trusted. The hash cell scheme isn't described.

stumbles.quote: Centroids from Lloyd and from e-means give the same recall to within 0.005, so the only difference between them is training time.
stumbles.why: This conflicts with the speed claim. It is unclear which recall (offset-coding or index-cell) is meant, and "only difference" is stronger than the data shown.

stumbles.quote: I had expected the offset coding to be the result and the index cells to be a side note. It came out the other way.
stumbles.why: Earlier the text says the author's expectation was faster training, not offset coding. The text never mentions an expectation about offset coding, so it reads as a contradiction of the earlier "main use" statement.

point: Using 4,096 k-means centroids (trained fast with e-means, though Lloyd's gives the same recall) as index cells found 90% of true neighbours while scanning 0.56% of the corpus, which is a bigger payoff than faster training or offset coding for quantization.
